title: Take Care of the People, the Products, and the Profits, In That Order

canonicalEdition.name: First edition
canonicalEdition.sourceProvenance: Frozen web bundle only: bibliographic records, table-of-contents evidence, official publication metadata, and narrow secondary summary support. Paraphrase-first; no full text frozen.

anchorSummary: Horowitz shifts from pure survival to company design, arguing that startups need real management systems around people and product long before neglect becomes visible in the profit line.
coreClaim: A company becomes durable when leaders invest in people development and product quality first, because profits depend on that operating order rather than replacing it.
distinctMechanism: Horowitz links culture, training, hiring, management debt, and management quality assurance into one argument: if you neglect the people system, both product and profit decay later.
requiredAnchors: A good place to work: culture has to support performance, not just comfort.
Training and executive hiring: startups cannot outsource managerial development forever.
Management debt: neglected people systems eventually create compounding operating problems.
specificApplications: Use training as a force multiplier instead of treating it as big-company overhead.
Recognize management debt before it compounds into culture and execution failures.
Tie people systems directly to product and business outcomes.
commonMisreadings: Reading the chapter as anti-profit rather than as an argument about the order that makes profit durable.
Reducing people care to perks while ignoring training, management quality, and role clarity.
hardEdgeRequirement: Hard mode must show how founders create expensive problems when they postpone management discipline because the startup still feels small.
thresholdQuestion: What breaks first when a company grows faster than its management system?
